rows.judge_notes: The biggest gap is a money pump: firing five cancel requests at once for one paid $25 booking sent five refunds totalling $125, because the refund is awaited before the booking is marked cancelled; in a separate test, cancelling a pending booking while its charge was still processing ended with that booking confirmed and charged. The strongest part is the HTTP layer: the price is set on the server, holds expire, the owner's refunds on cancelling a class are retried safely, writes use temp-file-and-rename, passwords are hashed with scrypt, the session cookie is httpOnly and SameSite, user text is never inserted as HTML, there is a CSP, and 11 end-to-end tests pass under node --test. It is not sellable: spec.md is only the one-sentence request with no journeys or acceptance criteria, the README is one line, there is no health endpoint, no login rate limit (10 bad owner logins in a row were all accepted for checking) and no real payment provider or webhook verification.

The biggest gaps: there is no spec beyond the one-sentence request (no roles, journeys or acceptance criteria) and no real ops support (the README is one line and there is no health endpoint), while payments use a mock provider with no signed or idempotent webhooks, auth uses a Bearer token kept in localStorage instead of httpOnly cookies, and nothing limits login attempts. The strongest part is the booking and payment logic: the server sets the price, a 10-minute seat hold and a payment-in-progress lock block double charges, a booking is confirmed only after a successful charge, refunds follow a clear 24-hour rule and owner cancellation, files are written atomically via temp-file-and-rename, and all 9 HTTP tests pass under node --test. Sellable: no.

The biggest gap is that spec.md is still the one-sentence request with no users, roles, journeys or acceptance criteria, so none of the 13 passing HTTP tests trace back to a specified journey. Beyond that, payments are only an offline test stub that sends raw card numbers to the server, with no webhooks or signature checks; customers cannot cancel their own bookings; the owner logs in with HTTP Basic auth against a plaintext password from the environment, with no rate limiting or CSRF protection; there is no health endpoint and no deploy guide. The strongest part is the booking core: the server sets the price at booking time, the synchronous single-process handlers prevent overbooking, seat holds expire after 15 minutes, owner cancellations refund once and change the booking status so they can't refund twice, the output is XSS-safe because it uses textContent, writes are atomic through temp-file-and-rename, and the end-to-end HTTP tests pass. Not sellable as is.

The biggest gap is that there is no live payment provider: only the test-only `local` provider exists, and production refuses to start unless ALLOW_TEST_PAYMENTS=true, in which case no real money moves. The strongest part is the money and integrity core: the server sets every amount, webhooks are HMAC-verified and deduplicated by charge id, refunds use idempotency keys, late or wrong-amount payments are refunded automatically, all writes go through one serialised transaction that cannot oversell, and writes are atomic (temp file, fsync, rename); all 15 specified journeys pass as HTTP end-to-end tests (102/102 under `node --test`). Sellable: not yet, because it cannot take real payments until a live provider adapter such as Stripe Checkout is written and verified, which should be a small job given the existing provider contract.

The biggest gap is that a customer gets no email and cannot reset a password, the UI and the Stripe integration were never run in a real browser or against live Stripe, and STUDIO_NAME is hardcoded rather than shown in the page header. The strongest part is the booking and payment core: held seats with deadlines, signed and deduplicated webhooks, refunds with idempotency keys that the sweep retries, and serialized atomic transactions; all 49 tests pass and a concurrency probe of 20 requests for 2 spots produced exactly 2 bookings. Sellable: yes for a small studio as a pilot, once someone runs a Stripe test-mode checkout and refund and adds email notifications.

The biggest gap is that there is no real payment provider: the only one that works is a local test provider, so customers pay by picking a 'Test card' in a dropdown, there are no signed webhooks, and `PAYMENT_PROVIDER=stripe` deliberately fails at startup, so the studio cannot take real money. The strongest part is the engineering: SPEC.md defines roles and 12 journeys (J1–J12) with acceptance criteria and failure paths, and all 98 tests pass under `node --test`, driving every journey over real HTTP. Those tests cover concurrent booking of the last seat, payment holds, refund failure and retry, and restart durability, backed by layered domain, service and HTTP code, server-side amounts, idempotency keys, a serialized store with atomic writes, scrypt hashing and signed httpOnly cookies. Sellable: no, not until a real provider such as Stripe, with verified webhooks, is added behind the existing payment interface.
